metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content: Immediately following a procedure, surgical personnel must wipe gross soil from instruments using a damp sterile sponge and spray instruments with an enzymatic pre-cleaner to prevent drying of organic matter.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content:
When processing soiled instruments in the CSSD decontamination area, technicians must execute the following sequential steps:
1. Don full decontamination PPE (heavy-duty nitrile gloves, fluid-resistant gown, face shield, and protective footwear).
2. Submerge instruments in an enzymatic detergent solution prepared at the manufacturer’s specified concentration and temperature.
3. Clean all surfaces, hinges, and lumens using soft-bristled brushes while fully submerged under water to prevent aerosol generation.
4. Rinse thoroughly with critical (purified) water to remove detergent residues.
5. Load instruments into the automated ultrasonic cleaner or washer-disinfector for full thermal disinfection cycles.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content:
1. Inspect cleaned instruments under magnification for cleanliness, alignment, and functionality.
2. Wrap instrument trays using double-layer non-woven polypropylene wrap or rigid sterilization containers.
3. Place a chemical indicator strip inside every package and apply external indicator tape to each wrapped tray.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content:
Dynamic Air Removal (Pre-vacuum) steam sterilizers must maintain the following minimum validated exposure parameters:
1. Temperature: **132°C (270°F)** for a minimum exposure time of **4 minutes** at 27 to 30 psi.
2. Alternative Temperature: **135°C (275°F)** for a minimum exposure time of **3 minutes**.
3. Minimum drying time: **20 to 30 minutes** post-sterilization cycle.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content:
1. Chemical Indicators: Verify color change on external tape and internal indicator before releasing any pack.
2. Biological Indicators: Perform a Biological Indicator (Geobacillus stearothermophilus) test at least daily for each autoclave, and in **every load containing implantable devices**.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content: If a biological indicator yields a positive result (indicating failure), the CSSD Supervisor must immediately halt autoclave operations, quarantine the unit, and recall all items processed in that autoclave since the last negative biological test.

metadata.document_title: Sterilization and Decontamination of Surgical Instruments

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines standardized cleaning and disinfection practices for Operating Rooms (OR) to maintain environmental cleanliness, control bioburden, and prevent surgical site infections (SSI).

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: This policy applies to all Environmental Services (EVS) personnel, perioperative support staff, and surgical nurses involved in environmental cleaning before, during, and after surgical procedures.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: The **EVS Operating Room Team Lead** is responsible for executing environmental cleaning protocols, verifying surface disinfection contact times, and documenting daily cleanliness logs.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: The **Operating Room Charge Nurse** verifies that turnover cleaning is complete and inspected prior to permitting the next surgical patient to enter the room.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: Before the first scheduled surgical procedure of the day, EVS staff must damp-dust all horizontal surfaces (surgical lights, boom arms, surgical tables, equipment carts) using a clean microfiber cloth moistened with EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: During a surgical procedure, any accidental blood or body fluid spills must be promptly contained and spot-cleaned by designated staff using an approved disinfectant.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content:
EVS personnel must perform the following sequential steps during room turnover between surgical procedures:
1. Don appropriate protective apparel, including fluid-resistant gloves and eye protection.
2. Collect and remove all regulated medical waste (biohazard bags) and linen bags, sealing them prior to transport.
3. Clean and disinfect all high-touch surfaces, including surgical lights, anesthesia carts, operating table pads, positioning devices, electrosurgical units, and suction canisters.
4. Clean the floor surrounding the operating table within a 3-to-4-foot perimeter, or further if visible contamination exists.
5. Apply EPA-registered intermediate-level disinfectant to all cleaned surfaces, ensuring the surface remains visibly wet for the full manufacturer-recommended **wet contact time (minimum 3 to 5 minutes)**.
6. Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and allow surfaces to completely air dry before placing fresh linens on the operating table.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: At the end of each working day, every operating room must undergo terminal cleaning, regardless of whether it was used. This includes scrubbing all walls, ceilings, light fixtures, scrub sinks, overhead tracks, and total floor flooding/mopping with a germicidal disinfectant solution.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: The EVS Team Lead must perform weekly random visual and fluorescent marker audits on high-touch surfaces in at least 25% of operating rooms to evaluate cleaning thoroughness and provide feedback to EVS staff.

metadata.document_title: Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection of Operating Rooms

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) specifies engineering controls, door-monitored pressure differentials, airflow requirements, and room assignment workflows for Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units to prevent airborne and droplet-borne pathogen transmission.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: This policy applies to facility engineers, infection control practitioners, nursing staff, and emergency department intake personnel across all inpatient care facilities.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: The **Facilities Lead Engineer** is responsible for continuously monitoring negative pressure HVAC systems, verifying Air Changes Per Hour (ACH), and performing daily differential pressure sensor calibrations.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: The **Infection Preventionist / Bed Placement Manager** is responsible for authorizing patient placement in AIIR units and enforcing isolation door status.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content:
1. Airflow Differential: Continuous negative pressure relative to the surrounding hallways and anterooms, maintaining a minimum pressure differential of **-2.5 Pascals (-0.01 inches water gauge)**.
2. Air Change Rate: A minimum of **12 Air Changes Per Hour (ACH)** for newly constructed or renovated facilities (minimum 6 ACH for existing facilities).
3. Exhaust Handling: Total air exhaust must be vented directly to the outside away from air intake vents, or filtered through high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtration units before recirculation.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: Facilities staff and nursing personnel must verify negative pressure prior to patient occupancy and daily thereafter using both continuous electronic pressure monitors and visual tissue/ball-in-tube indicators.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content:
When admitting or transferring a patient requiring airborne isolation, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Contact the Bed Placement Manager to identify an available, verified negative-pressure AIIR.
2. Confirm negative pressure status on the anteroom gauge before transferring the patient.
3. Place a surgical mask on the patient during transport to the isolation room.
4. Escort the patient into the AIIR and ensure both anteroom and main isolation doors remain completely closed.
5. Post designated "Airborne Isolation Precautions" signage outside the entry door.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: Anteroom doors and primary AIIR doors must never be open simultaneously. Anteroom doors must automatically close and latch after entry or exit.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: After an airborne isolation patient is discharged, the room door must remain closed, and the room must remain vacant with negative pressure running for a specific clearance time based on ACH (e.g., **45 minutes at 12 ACH**) to allow 99.9% airborne contaminant removal prior to terminal cleaning.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: Facilities engineers must inspect, test, and replace HEPA filters in AIIR exhaust systems every **6 months** or whenever pressure differential across the filter indicates saturation.

metadata.document_title: Management of Airborne Infection Isolation Rooms (AIIR) and Droplet Isolation Units

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines standardized activation channels, team response roles, and immediate execution workflows for hospital-wide emergency codes to safeguard patients, visitors, and staff during acute clinical or facility emergencies.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content: This policy applies to all clinical nursing staff, attending physicians, security personnel, facility engineers, emergency department staff, and central switchboard operators across all inpatient wards, outpatient clinics, and administrative buildings.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content: The **Emergency Operations Center (EOC) / Telecommunications Operator** is responsible for receiving emergency call notifications, broadcasting code announcements overhead, and dispatching designated response teams within designated response timeframes.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content: The **Rapid Response Team (RRT) Lead / Code Blue Captain** is responsible for assuming command of clinical resuscitations upon arrival at the emergency scene.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content:
1. **Code Blue:** Cardiac or respiratory arrest involving an adult or pediatric patient.
2. **Code Red:** Fire, smoke discovery, or active thermal alarm activation.
3. **Code Pink:** Infant or pediatric abduction / missing child alert.
4. **Code Black:** Bomb threat or suspicious package discovery.
5. **Code Grey:** Aggressive, violent, or combative individual requiring immediate intervention.
6. **Code Silver:** Active shooter or weapon-bearing hostile individual.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content:
When a clinician discovers a patient in cardiac or respiratory arrest, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Verify unresponsiveness and absence of pulse/breathing.
2. Dial the internal emergency extension (**ext. 5555**) or push the wall-mounted Code Blue alarm button.
3. State to the operator: "Code Blue, [Building Name], [Floor Number], [Room/Location]".
4. Initiate immediate chest compressions and basic life support (BLS) steps.
5. Obtain the nearest Automated External Defibrillator (AED) / Crash Cart.
6. Switchboard operator broadcasts "Code Blue, Room [X]" overhead **three times** and automatically pages the Rapid Response Team.
7. Code Blue Team arrives on site within **3 minutes**, and the Code Captain assumes ALS leadership.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols
metadata.section_title: Code Activation and Resuscitation Response Workflow

page_content:
Upon notification of a suspected infant abduction:
1. Call ext. 5555 to declare "Code Pink" with patient description and last known location.
2. Switchboard broadcasts "Code Pink" overhead across all hospital sectors.
3. Security personnel immediately lock down all facility perimeter doors, stairwells, and elevator banks.
4. Staff check all hallways, exit corridors, and restrooms within their assigned departments for unauthorized carry bags or individuals matching the alert description.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols
metadata.section_title: Code Activation and Resuscitation Response Workflow

page_content: Only the designated Incident Commander, Code Captain, or Security Lead may authorize the Telecommunications Operator to broadcast an "All Clear" announcement overhead.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content: Following any emergency code activation, the initiating nurse and response team lead must complete the online Emergency Code Evaluation Form in the EHR within **12 hours** to support continuous quality improvement.

metadata.document_title: Emergency Code Activation and Response Protocols

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines disaster triage operational structures, surge capacity expansion protocols, and patient categorization models during external or internal Mass Casualty Incidents (MCI).

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: This policy applies to all emergency department physicians, trauma surgeons, disaster response teams, triage nurses, security staff, and hospital administrative leadership.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: The **Emergency Department Triage Officer (Attending Physician or Senior ER Nurse)** is responsible for performing rapid triage categorizations at the intake decontamination zone and directing patient flow.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: The **Hospital Incident Commander (Chief Medical Officer / ED Director)** is responsible for activating the Hospital Emergency Operations Center (HEOC) and declaring internal disaster response levels.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: Staff must utilize the **Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment (START)** protocol for adult patients (or JumpSTART for pediatric victims) to categorize casualties within **60 seconds per patient**.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content:
1. **RED Tag (Immediate):** Severe life-threatening injuries requiring immediate intervention within 15–30 minutes (e.g., airway compromise, tension pneumothorax, uncontrolled severe hemorrhage).
2. **YELLOW Tag (Delayed):** Serious injuries requiring medical care within 1 to 2 hours, but stable without immediate life threat (e.g., non-compromised open fractures, controlled soft tissue trauma).
3. **GREEN Tag (Minor / Walking Wounded):** Minor injuries where care can be safely deferred for several hours; patients can ambulate independently.
4. **BLACK Tag (Expectant / Deceased):** Deceased victims or catastrophic injuries where survival is unlikely even with maximal intervention (e.g., massive brain tissue destruction, absent pulse/spontaneous respirations after airway opening).

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content:
Upon notification of an incoming mass casualty event from local Emergency Medical Services (EMS), staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. The ED Attending Physician notifies the Hospital Administrator on Call and declares a "Code Yellow (MCI Activation)".
2. Activate the Hospital Emergency Operations Center (HEOC) and assign Incident Command roles.
3. Establish external triage posts outside the ambulance bay entrance to screen incoming arrivals.
4. Convert the Emergency Department treatment bays to RED category resuscitation zones.
5. Re-allocate stable inpatient beds by expediting discharge of low-acuity ward patients to holding areas.
6. Station Triage Nurses at intake gates to apply color-coded triage tags and wristbands to all incoming casualties prior to hospital entry.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: The Hospital Incident Commander authorizes termination of MCI status once all incoming casualties have been triaged, stabilized, and assigned to definitive treatment areas or surgical suites.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: Within **48 hours** of disaster de-activation, the Disaster Management Committee must convene a formal hot-debriefing session and submit an After-Action Report (AAR) to the Board of Directors.

metadata.document_title: Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) and Disaster Triage Protocol

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines standardized safety requirements, clinical handoff workflows, and equipment monitoring protocols for transporting inpatients between departments, diagnostic suites, or intensive care units within the facility.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: This policy applies to all registered nurses, respiratory therapists, transport technicians, radiology staff, and attending physicians involved in intra-facility patient movement.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: The **Sending Primary Nurse** is responsible for conducting the pre-transport stability assessment, preparing portable monitoring equipment, and performing structured handoff communication with the receiving unit.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: The **Transport Escort (RN or Respiratory Therapist)** is responsible for continuously monitoring vital signs, managing active line infusions, and maintaining airway stability during transit.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content:
1. **Low Risk (Unmonitored):** Transport Technician or Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) for stable patients requiring routine diagnostic imaging.
2. **Moderate Risk (Telemetry / IV Therapy):** Registered Nurse (RN) required for patients with active telemetry, continuous IV drips, or high risk of acute deterioration.
3. **High Risk (ICU / Mechanical Ventilation):** Critical Care RN and Respiratory Therapist (RT) required for intubated patients, patients receiving continuous vasoactive infusions, or patients with invasive arterial monitoring.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety
metadata.section_title: Transport Escalation Tiers and Personnel Requirements

page_content:
Prior to moving any patient out of a clinical care unit, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Re-assess patient vital signs and clinical stability within **15 minutes** prior to departure.
2. Verify that portable oxygen tanks have at least **500 psi** of pressure remaining (or sufficient volume for twice the estimated transport time).
3. Secure all IV lines, urinary drainage bags, and chest tubes below the level of the patient's torso.
4. Perform verbal **SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)** handoff with the receiving department clinician via telephone or secure direct contact.
5. Place the patient on a portable battery-powered cardiac monitor/defibrillator for all telemetry or ICU transfers.
6. Transport the patient using the primary bed or high-sided stretcher with all side rails locked in the upright position.
7. Upon arrival at the receiving unit, conduct bedside handoff and re-verify vital signs before transferring primary care responsibility.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: If a patient experiences severe acute clinical deterioration, cardiac arrest, or accidental extubation during transit in a hallway or elevator, the escort team must immediately stop, activate the nearest wall emergency alarm or call ext. 5555 for an emergency response, and initiate basic resuscitation.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: The sending nurse must log the departure time, escort names, baseline vitals, and arrival handoff completion in the patient's electronic health record within **1 hour** post-transport.

metadata.document_title: Patient Transfer and Intra-Facility Transport Safety

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines mandatory containment, handling, storage, and disposal protocols for biohazardous waste, chemical agents, cytotoxic pharmaceuticals, and radioactive materials to protect hospital personnel and ensure compliance with environmental safety regulations.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: This policy applies to all environmental services (EVS) staff, laboratory technicians, clinical nurses, pharmacists, nuclear medicine specialists, and facility engineers across all hospital care settings and diagnostic laboratories.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: The **Environmental Services (EVS) Safety Lead / Lab Safety Officer** is responsible for overseeing hazardous waste collection schedules, inspect storage receptacles, and maintaining Safety Data Sheets (SDS).

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: The **Clinical Staff / Technician** generating the waste is responsible for correctly segregating and disposing of hazardous materials at the immediate point of origin.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content:
1. **Regulated Medical Waste (Biohazard):** Contaminated dressings, blood products, and tissue placed in leak-proof **Red Biohazard Bags**.
2. **Sharps Waste:** Needles, scalpels, lancets, and broken glass vials placed directly into puncture-resistant, rigid **Red/Yellow Sharps Containers**.
3. **Trace Chemotherapy Waste:** Empty vials, IV bags, and gloves used in cytotoxic administration placed in rigid **Yellow Trace Waste Bins**.
4. **Pharmaceutical Waste:** Expired or partially used non-controlled medications placed in **Blue Pharmaceutical Containers**.
5. **Radioactive Waste:** Isotope containers and radio-contaminated materials managed in lead-shielded **Radioactive Storage Bins**.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal
metadata.section_title: Waste Segregation Categories and Color Standards

page_content:
When a hazardous chemical or biohazardous fluid spill occurs, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Evacuate the immediate area and restrict access to prevent exposure.
2. Consult the specific **Safety Data Sheet (SDS)** located in the electronic portal or binder.
3. Don appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including chemical-resistant gloves, eye protection/face shield, and fluid-resistant apron.
4. Obtain the standardized **Hazardous Materials Spill Kit** from the designated clean utility room.
5. Apply absorbent spill-lock powder or containment booms around the perimeter of the liquid spill.
6. Scoop up absorbed material using non-sparking tools and place into designated hazardous disposal bags.
7. Decontaminate the affected surface using an approved high-level disinfectant solution (e.g., 1:10 sodium hypochlorite dilution).
8. Remove PPE in the proper order and place contaminated gear inside the biohazard waste bag.
9. Notify the EVS Safety Lead and submit an Environmental Incident Report within **4 hours**.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: Hazardous waste storage rooms must remain locked, temperature-controlled, clearly labeled with biohazard warnings, and accessible only to authorized personnel.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: All hazardous waste removed by licensed external disposal contractors must be logged with signed Hazardous Waste Manifests maintained by the Facilities Department for a minimum of **3 years**.

metadata.document_title: Hazardous Materials Handling and Waste Disposal

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines standards for preventive maintenance, pre-use safety inspections, and clinical alarm configuration to prevent equipment failures and eliminate alarm fatigue across patient care environments.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content: This policy applies to biomedical engineering technicians, clinical care nurses, respiratory therapists, surgical technologists, and unit leaders utilizing or servicing medical devices across all inpatient and outpatient facilities.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content: The **Biomedical Engineering Department** is responsible for performing scheduled Preventive Maintenance (PM), tracking device inspection cycles, and certifying clinical equipment safety.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content: The **Bedside Clinical Care Nurse** is responsible for verifying device operational integrity before patient attachment, setting customized alarm parameters, and responding promptly to active visual and audible alerts.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content:
1. Every clinical medical device (e.g., infusion pumps, patient monitors, ventilators, defibrillators) must display a valid, updated green **"Passed Biomedical Inspection" tag** indicating the next inspection due date.
2. Any device lacking a valid inspection tag or past its inspection due date must be removed from clinical service immediately.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content: When a medical device malfunctions or displays error codes, staff must immediately apply a red **"OUT OF SERVICE - DEFECTIVE" tag**, remove the device from patient areas, and log a service ticket with Biomedical Engineering.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content:
To prevent alarm fatigue and ensure critical physiological alarms receive rapid clinical attention:
1. Default alarm thresholds must be customized to fit individual patient clinical baseline parameters at the start of each shift.
2. Secondary or non-actionable notification volumes must be adjusted appropriately, while critical life-threatening alarm volume must remain audible above background room noise.
3. Electrodes and sensor cables must be replaced according to manufacturer guidelines to reduce false artifact alarms.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content:
Prior to placing any clinical equipment on a patient, clinical staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Visually inspect power cords, casings, and display panels for physical damage or wear.
2. Confirm presence of a current Biomedical PM green sticker.
3. Plug the device into an emergency backup power outlet (red wall receptacle).
4. Power on the device and verify successful completion of the automated self-test sequence.
5. Confirm alarm limits are enabled, set to patient-appropriate parameters, and set to active audibility mode.
6. Document equipment operational verification in the EHR setup checklist.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management

page_content: If a medical device failure results in or contributes to patient injury, near-miss, or death, staff must immediately preserve all settings, disconnect the device from the patient, seal the unit without altering control knobs/drips, and notify Bio-Medical Engineering and Risk Management.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management
metadata.section_title: Adverse Incident Reporting and Device Sequestration

page_content: The Hospital Safety Officer must report device-related serious injuries or deaths to the device manufacturer and relevant regulatory authorities within **10 business days**.

metadata.document_title: Clinical Equipment Maintenance and Alarm Safety Management
metadata.section_title: Adverse Incident Reporting and Device Sequestration

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines immediate response protocols, auxiliary system switchover sequences, and operational continuity workflows during catastrophic interruptions of critical hospital utilities, including electrical power, municipal water, medical gases, and HVAC systems.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content: This policy applies to facility engineers, emergency command personnel, clinical nursing supervisors, intensive care units, operating room staff, and administrative leads across all hospital facilities.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content: The **Director of Facility Operations / Chief Engineer** is responsible for monitoring primary utility feeds, verifying automatic backup system activations, and managing physical infrastructure repairs.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content: The **Inpatient Nursing Supervisor / Administrative Director on Call** is responsible for managing clinical load balancing, coordinating portable life-support support, and executing internal evacuation plans if necessary.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content:
1. Critical life-safety circuits and red emergency power receptacles are backed up by emergency diesel generators.
2. Generator automatic transfer switches (ATS) must restore emergency electrical power to red outlets within **10 seconds** of primary utility loss.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content:
1. Secondary bulk oxygen reserve manifolds automatically initiate flow if primary liquid oxygen line pressure drops below **40 psi**.
2. Auxiliary zone valve boxes must remain accessible to designated charge nurses at all times.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content:
Upon sudden loss of main electrical power, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Verify emergency generator activation within 10 seconds (confirm illumination of red emergency outlets).
2. Plug all critical life-sustaining devices (ventilators, infusion pumps, intra-aortic balloon pumps) directly into red emergency power outlets.
3. Obtain portable emergency LED lighting units stored in clean utility rooms for unlit hallways and nursing stations.
4. Assess ventilated patients to confirm continuous mechanical function; switch to manual bag-valve-mask (Ambu bag) ventilation if ventilator battery power drops below critical levels.
5. Facilities staff perform manual inspection of all emergency generator transfer switches and fuel tank levels.
6. Central Switchboard announces "Code Yellow - Utility Emergency (Electrical)" to initiate incident command protocols if outage exceeds 15 minutes.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content:
In the event of sudden main oxygen line pressure loss:
1. Charge Nurse immediately retrieves emergency E-cylinder portable oxygen tanks from the unit storage room.
2. Switch intubated or high-flow oxygen patients from wall outlets to portable E-cylinders.
3. Facility operations manually switch bulk oxygen supply to secondary reserve manifolds.
4. If pipeline rupture occurs within a specific unit, the designated unit nurse manually closes the local zone valve box to isolate the leak.

metadata.document_title: Utility Failure and Back-Up System Activation Protocols

page_content: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines physical security standards, visitor access control procedures, badge identification requirements, and restricted area protocols to ensure a safe environment for patients, staff, and visitors.

page_content: This policy applies to all security officers, reception staff, clinical nursing leads, facility management, and administrative personnel across all hospital access portals, inpatient wards, and specialized care units.

metadata.document_title: Visitor Control and Physical Security Protocols

page_content: The **Director of Security / Security Officers** are responsible for managing perimeter access checkpoints, issuing visitor passes, monitoring electronic surveillance networks, and responding to physical security threats.

metadata.document_title: Visitor Control and Physical Security Protocols

page_content: The **Unit Clerk / Charge Nurse** is responsible for verifying visitor credentials at specialized care unit entrances, enforcing unit visiting hours, and monitoring visitor compliance within patient care areas.

metadata.document_title: Visitor Control and Physical Security Protocols

page_content:
1. General inpatient visiting hours are established from **08:00 to 20:00 daily**.
2. Standard inpatient units permit a maximum of **two (2) visitors** per patient at any single time.
3. Intensive Care Units (ICU) and Emergency Departments permit a maximum of **one (1) visitor** at the bedside, subject to clinical team discretion.

metadata.document_title: Visitor Control and Physical Security Protocols

page_content: All visitors entering hospital facilities must present a valid government-issued photo ID at main security reception checkpoints to receive a photo-printed **Visitor Pass Badge**. The badge must be worn visibly above the waist at all times while on hospital premises.

metadata.document_title: Visitor Control and Physical Security Protocols

page_content:
Upon arrival at any hospital entrance after general hours or at specialized unit portals, staff must execute the following sequential workflow:
1. Security or reception staff request government-issued photo identification from the visitor.
2. Search the EHR visitor management module to confirm the patient permits visitors and has not placed a "Do Not Disclose" security restriction on their file.
3. Log visitor full name, contact number, and destination room into the electronic Visitor Management System.
4. Capture visitor photo and print an adhesive Visitor Pass Badge displaying the current date, visitor name, and designated destination.
5. Instruct the visitor to apply the badge prominently to their outerwear.
6. Verify badge validity at unit access points via electronic scanner or visual inspection prior to granting entry.
